title: Muse Spark 1.1 evaluation framework for cheapest-correct-model routing
description: Build a bounded Meta Model API adapter and a reproducible cross-model benchmark packet that can support exactly one terminal disposition (REJECTED, BOUNDED_USE, or PROMOTED_WITH_SCOPE), ensuring correctness, safety, privacy, latency, reliability, and governance gates are satisfied before promotion.
pain_point: Vendor claims are not verified operating facts; there is a need to separate vendor-announced capability, third-party evaluation, locally observed benchmark results, and inferences. Without a rigorous benchmark, there is risk of silent paid-model fallback, authority-boundary failures, or promoting a model based on unsubstantiated marketing claims.
use_case: Evaluating whether Muse Spark 1.1 belongs in the HUMMBL / Ownward model-routing stack under the doctrine that the cheapest correct model wins only after correctness, safety, privacy, latency, reliability, and governance gates are satisfied. The evaluation requires a provider adapter, policy declaration, and fixed benchmark packet across multiple lanes including MCP reliability, governed delegation, repository execution, long-context integrity, computer-use safety, and cost-adjusted correctness.

When the inbox grows too long or starts truncating, rotate to a fresh exact-latest inbox before asking Sergio for more review.

title: Deterministic game loop stepping for headless verification of physics/animation apps
description: The platform's `page eval` headless browser cannot run a real-time canvas game render loop at speed, causing false negatives. The warning suggests stepping the app's own loop deterministically, but no CLI or skill provides this capability. Agents are forced to abandon real-time verification, leaving core mechanics (brick collision, scoring, lives) unverified.
pain_point: The verify step is the only step with no working tool for canvas/physics/animation apps. The ball never travels far enough in real time to hit bricks, so bricks stay at 60 and score at 0 across every sample. The agent had no follow-up move after the warning; it abandoned the approach entirely, leaving brick collision, scoring, lives, and win/game-over screens unverified.
use_case: Agent built a Phaser brick-breaker game and tries to verify the real gameplay loop (ball bounces, bricks break, score increments, lives decrement) by driving the deployed page with `gipity page eval`. It samples ball position over time, but on the third eval that would confirm brick collision and score change, the platform returns a warning about slow render (14.5 fps) and advises stepping the app's loop deterministically. The agent has no tool to do that, so it drops real-time verification, takes a static screenshot, and ships the game with its core mechanic never exercised.

title: Fix Direct Codex documentation to match actual agent lifecycle and slot count

This mismatch causes failures when following documented steps. The user proposes transitioning to a capability-based lifecycle and slot contract, creating current/legacy/unknown profiles based on actual tool availability.
pain_point: Documentation states non-existent `close_agent` and incorrect number of threads (6 vs 4), causing orchestration code that follows the documentation to fail at runtime (e.g., calling `close_agent` that doesn't exist or launching 4 FULL reviewers as a batch and failing due to slot limit). The mismatch between advertised surface and actual surface makes documented steps untrustworthy and requires manual probing or workarounds.
use_case: Developer writing agent orchestration code using Direct Codex must rely on documentation (runtime-mapping.md, AGENTS.override.md) to know available functions and thread limits. The documented interface promises `spawn_agent → wait_agent → close_agent` with 6 threads, but the actual codex-cli 0.144.1 provides `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, `list_agents` without explicit close and only 4 active slots.

Preserve structured action data for expanded/session/model-visible representations.

title: Fix gh shim recursion when multiple aidevops shims exist on PATH
description: The aidevops 'gh' shim recursively selects another aidevops 'gh' shim as its downstream executable when a long-running session has an immutable runtime-bundle shim and a mutable installed shim both ahead of native GitHub CLI on PATH. This causes infinite recursion and timeout, blocking issue reads, claims, PR operations, diagnostics, pulse routines, and any framework helper that invokes ordinary 'gh'. The documented bypass AIDEVOPS_GH_SHIM_DISABLE=1 also fails because it uses the same defective resolver.
pain_point: The shim's resolver only excludes its own directory in `_find_real_gh()`, so with two shim generations it selects the other shim instead of native `gh`. The recursion causes infinite loop until external timeout kills the process, making all gh operations fail (blocking issue reads, claims, PR operations, diagnostics, pulse routines). Even the emergency bypass `AIDEVOPS_GH_SHIM_DISABLE=1` uses the same defective resolver and also recurses. Users must manually invoke `/usr/bin/gh` with a sanitized PATH as workaround.
use_case: In a long-running session with PATH starting with an immutable runtime-bundle agents/scripts directory and a mutable installed agents/scripts directory later on PATH (both containing the aidevops gh shim, but native gh is after both), running `gh --version` or any gh command results in recursive shim selection between the two wrappers, leading to timeout (exit code 124) rather than executing native GitHub CLI.

Additionally, managing state and preserving intent becomes complex when the user enters multiple follow-up or unexpected clarification questions, as a single tool must handle all such queries gracefully after initial invocation.

Need to implement a follow-up confirmation step: user first triggers a tool, then the system asks for confirmation; user replies with 'yes' or 'proceed', but the RAG system fails to select the correct tool because these confirmations lack context. The MCP server logs show tools are registered, but when sending tools/list or custom tool requests (e.g., getJob) from a Python client via SSE, the server receives the request but does not send any response back to the SSE queue, causing the client to time out.

User sends JSON-RPC requests like tools/list or calls a custom tool (e.g., getJob) and expects the server to return tool definitions or execution results via SSE, but the POST reaches the server and is mapped to WebMvcSseServerTransportProvider, yet no response comes back, causing the Python client to time out.
